\chapter{Making a Case --- Claim, Example, However, Although}
\label{ch:argumentar}
\hlchaptermodality{270}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can state an opinion in Spanish, back it with an example, turn against an objection, and grant one before I turn it.}

Complete ES-C270-aunque: run the four moves in order on one claim of your own.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[en mi opinión]{en mi opinión — marking a claim as yours}

\label{lesson:ES-C270-en-mi-opinion}



\begin{quote}
You can say what happened and how it felt. This chapter is for saying what you THINK, and defending it.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item durante — the last word of the experience chapter.
  \item creer — you can already say \emph{creo}, \textquotedblleft{}I believe.\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item Five syllables, and the accent on \emph{opinión} is doing the usual work: \emph{en-mi-o-pi-NIÓN}. $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{en mi opinión} — \textquotedblleft{}in my opinion.\textquotedblright{}

\emph{Opinión} is Latin \textbf{opinari}, \textquotedblleft{}to suppose, to think\textquotedblright{} — and the \emph{-ión} ending is the same one you met in \emph{habitación}, turning a verb into the noun for its result. An opinion is \emph{a supposing}, made into a thing you can hand someone.

English took the identical word from the identical place, which is why you can read it before you can say it.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
There is a difference between saying something and \textbf{marking it as a claim}, and this phrase does the marking. \emph{Es difícil} asserts that a thing is hard. \emph{En mi opinión, es difícil} says the same and hands the listener a place to disagree.

That is what makes it the opening move of an argument rather than a statement of fact — you are inviting the reply.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{en mi opinión}
  \item a claim with it — \emph{en mi opinión, es difícil}
  \item the same claim WITHOUT it, and hear the difference
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What Latin verb is \emph{opinión} built on? (\emph{Opinari}, \textquotedblleft{}to suppose.\textquotedblright{}) What does marking a claim as an opinion invite? (Disagreement — a reply.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[por ejemplo]{por ejemplo — the claim, and then the reason to believe it}

\label{lesson:ES-C270-por-ejemplo}



\begin{quote}
A claim on its own is just an assertion. This is how you back it.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item en mi opinión — the claim this supports.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{por e-JEM-plo}. The \emph{j} is the throat-sound you have met in \emph{trabajo}. $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{por ejemplo} — \textquotedblleft{}for example.\textquotedblright{}

\emph{Ejemplo} is Latin \textbf{exemplum}, and \emph{exemplum} is worth taking apart: \emph{ex-} (\textquotedblleft{}out of\textquotedblright{}) plus a root meaning \textquotedblleft{}to take.\textquotedblright{} An example is \textbf{a thing taken out} — one item lifted from a pile so the pile can be understood through it.

English \textbf{exemplary}, \textbf{sample} and \textbf{example} are all the same word arriving by different routes; \emph{sample} is the most worn-down of the three.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
This is the second move of an argument, and the order matters: claim first, example second. \emph{En mi opinión, es difícil. Por ejemplo, …}

An example is not proof — it is one thing taken out of the pile, which is exactly what the word says. That is worth knowing in both languages.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{por ejemplo}
  \item a claim, then an example — two sentences
  \item what \emph{exemplum} means literally (a thing taken out)
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{exemplum} mean, taken apart? (A thing taken \emph{out} of a pile.) Which comes first, the claim or the example? (The claim.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[sin embargo]{sin embargo — however, and why it is not pero}

\label{lesson:ES-C270-sin-embargo}



\begin{quote}
You have \emph{pero}, "but." This is its heavier cousin, and the difference is real.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item por ejemplo — the evidence move.
  \item pero — the ordinary \textquotedblleft{}but\textquotedblright{} you already own.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{sin em-BAR-go}. $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{sin embargo} — \textquotedblleft{}however, nevertheless.\textquotedblright{}

Literally \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}without hindrance.\textquotedblright{}} \emph{Embargo} is a hindrance, a seizure, an impediment — the same word English borrowed whole for a trade \textbf{embargo}, and it traces to a Latin-derived \emph{imbarricare}, \textquotedblleft{}to bar in.\textquotedblright{}

So the phrase says: \emph{that obstacle notwithstanding}. Whatever was just conceded, it does not stop what comes next.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
\emph{Pero} joins two things inside one breath: \emph{es difícil pero me gusta}.

\emph{Sin embargo} stands at the head of its own sentence and turns against everything before it: \emph{Es difícil. Sin embargo, me gusta.}

The second is what an argument needs, because you have to grant the other side's point in full before you turn it. \emph{Pero} is too light to carry that weight, which is why one is not a translation of the other.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{sin embargo}
  \item the light version — \emph{es difícil pero me gusta}
  \item the heavy version — two sentences, the second opening with \emph{sin embargo}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{sin embargo} mean literally? (Without hindrance.) What English word is \emph{embargo}? (The same one — a trade embargo.) Which of the two turns against a whole sentence rather than half of one? (\emph{Sin embargo}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[aunque]{aunque — conceding first, and arguing after}

\label{lesson:ES-C270-aunque}



\begin{quote}
The last move: granting the other side's point BEFORE you make yours.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item sin embargo — conceding after the fact.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{AUN-que}, two syllables. The \emph{au-} is one glide, not two vowels. $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{aunque} — \textquotedblleft{}although, even though.\textquotedblright{}

It is \emph{aun} (\textquotedblleft{}even, still\textquotedblright{}) welded to \emph{que} (\textquotedblleft{}that\textquotedblright{}), and \emph{aun} descends from Latin \textbf{adhuc}, \textquotedblleft{}up to this point, still.\textquotedblright{} So \emph{aunque} is, at root, \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}even that\textquotedblright{}} — even granting that.

You have watched this fusion happen twice already: \emph{ayer} out of \emph{ad heri}, and \emph{hablaré} out of \emph{hablar habeo}. Spanish builds most of its small words this way, by saying two words often enough that they become one.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
\emph{Sin embargo} concedes after: \emph{Es difícil. Sin embargo, me gusta.} \emph{Aunque} concedes first: \emph{Aunque es difícil, me gusta.}

Same two ideas, opposite order — and the order chooses what the listener remembers, because the sentence lands on whatever comes last. Leading with \emph{aunque} puts your own point in the emphatic position.

With that, you have the four moves: state a claim, support it, turn against an objection, and grant one before you turn it.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{aunque}
  \item the concession first — \emph{aunque es difícil, me gusta}
  \item all four moves in order — claim, example, however, although
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What two words is \emph{aunque} built from? (\emph{Aun} and \emph{que}.) Which Latin word is \emph{aun}? (\emph{Adhuc}, \textquotedblleft{}still.\textquotedblright{}) Which of \emph{aunque} and \emph{sin embargo} concedes first? (\emph{Aunque}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
